item.title: Posterior-anterior striatal reorganization after weight restoration in anorexia nervosa is associated with remission outcome: from mice to longitudinal human study
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric disorder with high relapse rates despite successful weight restoration. Altered reward processing and an imbalance between goal-directed and habitual control within the striatum have been proposed to contribute to the persistence of maladaptive behaviours, but the striatal mechanisms underlying recovery and relapse remain unclear. Here, we combined cross-species structural MRI with longitudinal clinical characterization to investigate striatal alterations associated with recovery from AN. Mice with deletion of the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChTcKO), a model of maladaptive eating behaviour, showed reduced dorsolateral striatal volume compared with wild-type mice. At baseline, women with AN (n = 71) showed reduced striatal volumes compared with healthy controls (n = 30). Longitudinally, patients with AN (n = 41) and healthy controls (n = 28) were reassessed, revealing substantial recovery of striatal volumes following weight restoration in AN. Posterior-anterior putamen gradient changes differed according to subsequent remission status, with changes in the right putamen gradient predicting relapse. Striatal gradient changes were also associated with goal-directed and habitual behaviour during the slip-of-action task, response consistency during delay discounting, and circulating ghrelin and desacyl ghrelin concentrations. These findings identify longitudinal putamen reorganization as a candidate marker of vulnerability to relapse and link striatal plasticity to reward-related and metabolic processes in AN.

item.title: Cumulative Prenatal Adversity and Fronto-Limbic White Matter Development Across Adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Importance: The prenatal period is a critical window for intergenerational transmission of adversity, yet the neural substrates through which cumulative prenatal stress becomes biologically embedded in offspring brain development remain poorly understood. White matter microstructure is a candidate mechanism linking prenatal adversity to downstream emotional dysregulation. Objective: To examine associations between cumulative adverse prenatal exposure (APE) burden and fronto-limbic white matter fractional anisotropy (FA) at baseline and across adolescent developmental trajectories, and to test whether white matter FA mediates prenatal APE effects on emotional dysregulation. Design, Setting, and Participants: Cohort study using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, Release 7.0, a diverse longitudinal cohort of US children recruited at ages 9 to 10 years across 21 sites. After diffusion tensor imaging quality control exclusions and retention of one twin or triplet per family, the final cross-sectional analytic sample comprised 10 483 participants. Longitudinal analyses included participants with data at one or more follow-up timepoints across four imaging waves. Exposures: Cumulative APE burden, operationalized as a sum of six binary adverse prenatal exposures (unplanned pregnancy; early alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis use before pregnancy recognition; complicated pregnancy; complicated birth; range, 0-6) following Zhi et al. (2026). Main Outcomes and Measures: Fractional anisotropy in 11 a priori fronto-limbic white matter tracts at baseline (ages approximately 10 years) and across four imaging timepoints (ages approximately 10, 12, 14, and 16 years). Exploratory outcomes included Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) dysregulation profile and Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ) subscales. Results: Higher prenatal APE burden was associated with lower baseline FA in left uncinate fasciculus (b = −0.00096; 95% CI, −0.00151 to −0.00042; FDR-corrected P = .006), corpus callosum (b = −0.00079; 95% CI, −0.00125 to −0.00032; FDR-corrected P = .006), and right uncinate fasciculus (b = −0.00071; 95% CI, −0.00120 to −0.00021; FDR-corrected P = .019). These associations were robust to adjustment for diffusion image quality, and prenatal burden was not associated with baseline image quality. In repeated-measures models across four imaging timepoints, higher APE burden was associated with steeper FA increases across adolescence (positive APE x Age interaction in 5 of 11 tracts; positive across all 11), though these trajectory effects were attenuated after adjustment for image quality. Post hoc analyses indicated that pregnancy complications and prenatal cannabis exposure were the most consistent contributors to these associations. White matter FA partially mediated the association between prenatal APE burden and involuntary emotional dysregulation, with no association with voluntary emotion regulation strategies. Conclusions and Relevance: Cumulative prenatal APE burden was associated with lower fronto-limbic white matter FA at the start of adolescence, an association that was stable across development and robust to image-quality adjustment. Evidence for altered developmental trajectories was more sensitive to image quality and should be interpreted cautiously. These findings identify fronto-limbic white matter-- particularly the uncinate fasciculus and corpus callosum-- as a candidate neurobiological correlate of cumulative prenatal adversity, while underscoring that this pathway reflects a bounded set of prenatal exposures.

item.title: Proteogenomics captures a midlife biological state of Alzheimer's disease susceptibility
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Alzheimer's disease (AD) develops over decades, but biological processes underlying susceptibility during midlife remain poorly understood. Using multimodal neuroimaging and plasma proteomics in UK Biobank participants, we identified circulating proteomic signatures of brain structure and organization. This 'neurostructural proteome' predicted future cognitive decline, incident dementia, and later-life AD pathology across independent cohorts spanning two decades of follow-up. Genetic and single-nucleus transcriptomic analyses demonstrated convergence of the neurostructural proteome and AD genetic architecture, highlighting enrichment in astrocyte, microglia, and endothelial pathways beyond the APOE region. Collectively, these findings identify a circulating neurostructural proteome detectable in midlife that captures molecular processes associated with future AD susceptibility and provide a framework for uncovering an early biological landscape of disease susceptibility that precedes conventional biomarkers and clinical onset.

item.title: Functional and Structural Brain Age Gaps as Complementary Predictive Markers for Cognitive Performance
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cognitive decline is characterized by substantial inter-individual variability across the lifespan, even among clinically healthy adults. However, it is unclear how structural and functional brain organization jointly relate to differences in cognitive performance within the typical populations. We considered a multimodal brain age framework by predicting for each subject its age from either structural MRI or resting-state functional MRI, after training on the 1000BRAINS cohort (901 participants, 18-85 years). Following, a structural and a functional brain age gap markers were defined as the deviations with respect to the real chronological age. We then used the markers to characterize the interplay between structure and function in shaping cognitive performances. Our findings reveal that the functional marker is as important to predict global cognitive performance as the structural marker. The most accurate prediction was found for global cognition, executive functions and episodic memory, followed by working memory, attention and language. In particular, the structural marker was contributing to all domains, except for working memory, whereas the functional marker had the highest contribution. Overall, structural and functional brain age models together provide a meaningful subject-level summary of brain information for predicting cognition, supporting a multidimensional view of typical aging.

item.title: Histological morphometric correlates of MRI-defined cortical thinning in temporal lobe epilepsy
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Large-scale MRI studies have consistently demonstrated progressive and age-accelerated neocortical thinning in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). These findings are frequently interpreted as evidence of cumulative neurodegeneration. However, the histopathological substrates underlying MRI-confirmed cortical thinning in epilepsy remain poorly defined. In particular, it is unknown whether cortical thinning reflects irreversible neuronal loss or potentially reversible epilepsy-related network alterations in cortical microstructure. We analysed the resected middle temporal gyrus from 117 individuals undergoing surgery for temporal lobe epilepsy, including cases with (n= 74) or without hippocampal sclerosis (HS) and 12 cases with additional temporal lobe sclerosis (TLS, or Focal Cortical Dysplasia IIIa), defined by a distinct pattern of cytoarchitectural reorganisation and gliosis involving superficial layers. All cases were stratified by the presence or absence of pre-operative MRI-defined cortical thinning of the middle temporal gyrus, quantified using CAT12 relative to healthy controls. On NeuN-immuno-labelled sections using automated image analysis we assessed neuronal spatial distributions relative to their size and packing density; relative cortical layer thickness and sulcal-gyral cytoarchitectural variation were also quantified. MRI-defined cortical thinning was not associated with diffuse neuronal loss. Instead, thinning correlated with increased neuronal density and altered cell-size spatial organisation in superficial and deep layers, particularly in right temporal lobe epilepsy cases with HS. There was limited evidence of layer-specific laminar thinning, being confined to layer VI in the right TLE/HS group only. Of note, TLS cases did not show either cortical thinning on MRI or laminar thinning on histology compared to cases without TLS but altered neuronal densities and composition that was not confined to the superficial cortex. MRI cortical thinning was also characterised by attenuation of normal sulcal/gyral cytoarchitectural variations suggesting disruption of cortical architectural gradients. In contrast, cases with HS but without MRI cortical thinning demonstrated loss of the expected inter-hemispheric cytoarchitectural asymmetry, indicating a distinct pathological process dissociated from thinning. Clinical-pathological correlations were lateralised, including age of onset, further supporting distinct mechanisms contributing to MRI cortical thinning between left and right TLE. These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that MRI-defined cortical thinning in epilepsy reflects progressive neuronal degeneration. Rather than laminar neuronal loss and atrophy, thinning was associated with altered neuronal packing and cell-size distributions between layers. This points towards altered neuropil volumes, including myelin content and dendritic remodelling, in turn suggesting potentially reversible dynamic seizure- or network-related processes.

item.title: The b-Value Dependence for Higher-Degree Spherical Harmonic Powers of the Diffusion MRI Signal Follows Stick Model Predictions in White Matter.
item.description:
Magnetic resonance in medicine
Purpose To compare the dependence on b-value of the spherical harmonic powers for the diffusion MRI signal in white matter to theoretical predictions from the stick model of water diffusion within axons. Methods Diffusion MRI data were acquired at 3 T in three healthy adults with 10 b-value shells (b = 1000-10 000 s/mm2 ) and 64 directions per shell. For every b-value, the signal was expanded in spherical harmonics for all even degrees l up to l = 6, and the harmonic power for each degree was calculated. These were compared in selected white matter regions of interest to the theoretical predictions of the stick model, which depend on just two adjustable parameters: the intra-axonal diffusivity and an amplitude factor for each degree. The intra-axonal diffusivity was estimated independently using triple diffusion encoding MRI, leaving the amplitude factor as the sole fitting parameter. Results Close agreement between experiment and theory was found for b ≳ 4000 s/mm2 , the threshold where extra-axonal water signal is expected to be strongly suppressed, for total cerebral white matter as well as separately within the genu, body, and splenium of the corpus callosum. These findings extend prior studies that either considered only the l = 0 harmonic power or treated the intra-axonal diffusivity as a fitting parameter. Conclusion In white matter, the b-value dependence of the diffusion MRI signal's even degree spherical harmonic powers up to l = 6 are relatively well-described by the stick model of axons for b ≳ 4000 s/mm2 .

item.title: Early-Life Environmental Exposures and Brain Structure in Schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Schizophrenia is widely considered a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by premorbid alterations in brain structure. Urban upbringing is a well-established environmental risk factor. However, urbanicity is often operationalised using broad population-based measures, leaving unclear which features of urban environments might affect the developing brain. This gap limits progress in understanding the pathways linking urban upbringing to schizophrenia, an increasingly important question as global urbanisation progresses. Cortical gyrification is especially informative in this context, as it is largely established before birth and remains relatively stable thereafter, offering a promising retrospective marker of early-life neurodevelopmental disturbances. Study Design: In this case-control MRI study, we examined whether residential environmental exposures at birth were associated with adult brain structure in 51 individuals with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and 88 healthy controls matched for age, sex and socioeconomic status. Birth addresses were linked to geospatial measures of air pollution, green space, built volume, built surface and population density. Study Results: Higher air pollution at birth was associated with lower cortical gyrification in individuals with schizophrenia, but not in healthy controls, particularly in orbitofrontal and inferior frontal regions. No comparable associations were observed for grey matter volume, cortical thickness or surface area. Conclusions: These findings suggest that air pollution at birth may be linked to hypogyria in schizophrenia and provide a potential bridge between epidemiological research on urbanicity and neurodevelopmental models of schizophrenia. In turn, this work provides a critical starting point for future work assessing how early urban environments become biologically embedded in schizophrenia risk.

item.title: Understanding cognitive function in post-COVID-19 condition with fatigue: an interdisciplinary multimodal investigation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Lingering cognitive symptoms of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) continue to challenge our understanding, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary research. We investigated whether individuals with PCC and fatigue differ from matched controls across neurocognitive, neuroimaging, and immunological measures, integrating these findings with qualitative phenomenological analyses through multimodal cross-analysis. Individuals with PCC and clinically significant fatigue (n=34), and age-, sex-, and education-matched controls recovered from COVID-19 without PCC (n=37) were included. Assessments encompassed physician evaluation, neuropsychological and functional tests, structural and functional MRI, immunological tests, and qualitative phenomenological analysis of interviews. Data were analyzed using established methods and an interdisciplinary cross-analysis to examine persistent cognitive symptoms in PCC. Group comparisons revealed subtle differences between individuals with PCC and controls, while neurocognitive performance and immunological markers remained within normative ranges. Modest differences in white matter, myelin related, and global brain measures were observed, alongside differences in associations between network connectivity and neurocognitive performance across groups, suggesting reduced network resilience rather than domain specific deficits. This pattern resonated with qualitative phenomenological findings: altered experiences of concentrating and difficulties to execute decisions and actions, despite preserved performance on standard neurocognitive tests. These findings suggest that cognitive symptoms in post-COVID-19 fatigue are associated with subtle neurobiological alterations not captured by standard cognitive assessments. In this highly fatigued sample, converging neuroimaging, neurocognitive and immunological findings point toward reduced network efficiency rather than overt cognitive impairment. Qualitative phenomenological analysis further highlighted altered modes of being in the world characterized by increased cognitive effort and difficulties executing decisions and actions.

item.title: Altered intersubject variability of functional connectivity in gray and white matter underlying neurocognition and genetic profiles in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.
item.description:
Neural regeneration research
Abstract Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is an autoimmune disease that causes inflammatory damage to the central nervous system. While alterations in functional connectivity have been reported in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, changes in intersubject variability of functional connectivity within gray matter and white matter are not yet understood. A total of 66 patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and 71 healthy controls were recruited. We compared intersubject variability of functional connectivity between patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and healthy controls and performed subgroup analyses comparing neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder patients with and without a history of optic neuritis. We also examined the associations between intersubject variability of functional connectivity alterations and disease duration, clinical disability, and cognitive scores. We combined our imaging results with those of the Allen Human Brain Atlas to conduct transcriptome-neuroimaging association analyses, identified gene expression profiles linked to intersubject variability of functional connectivity alterations and characterized their potential biological functions. Compared with healthy controls, patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder showed widespread increases in intersubject variability of functional connectivity. Notable gray matter alterations included the precentral and postcentral gyri; extensive occipital areas; and the insula, putamen, and thalamus. The corresponding white matter changes involved the fornix, corticospinal tract, widespread corona radiata, cingulum, and uncinate fasciculus. Compared with patients without optic neuritis, the optic neuritis subgroup exhibited distinct intersubject variability of functional connectivity alterations in specific regions, such as the inferior parietal lobule, angular gyrus, thalamus, fornix, and internal capsule. Clinically, only white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity correlated significantly with physical disability and cognitive processing speed and was not significantly associated with disease duration. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that genes positively associated with white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity were enriched in synaptic plasticity and cognition, while negatively associated genes were enriched in oxidative stress. Additionally, genes positively associated with the gray matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity were enriched in myelination and lipid biosynthesis, whereas genes negatively associated with the gray matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity were involved in synapse organization. In conclusion, our study revealed alterations in gray matter- and white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity across neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and clinical subtypes. We demonstrate that changes in white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity correlate with clinical disability and neurocognition. Linking these connectivity patterns with gene expression profiles may provide insights into the underlying pathophysiology of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.

item.title: Pain mechanisms in trigeminal neuralgia: From peripheral pathology to brain network reorganization and neurosurgical implications.
item.description:
Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
Objectives Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) involves peripheral neurovascular pathology and may also be associated with maladaptive neuroplastic changes in central nervous system networks. This review synthesizes evidence on peripheral and central pain mechanisms, neuroimaging biomarkers, molecular and transcriptomic correlates, and neurosurgical implications, including emerging neuromodulation strategies. Materials and methods This narrative review drew on topic-oriented searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science conducted between June 27 and July 5, 2026, covering literature published through June 2026. Supplementary targeted searches and reference-list screening were used to identify relevant publications. Evidence was synthesized qualitatively. Results Evidence supports a multilevel model of TN involving peripheral pathology and central neuroplastic changes. Neuroimaging studies report structural and functional alterations in sensorimotor, salience, limbic, and default mode networks, alongside disrupted structure-function coupling. Partial restoration of functional connectivity after neurosurgical treatment has been reported, although outcomes vary. Transcriptomic findings link imaging abnormalities to genes involved in ion channel function, synaptic signaling, neuroinflammation, and energy metabolism but remain hypothesis-generating. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) may provide short-term analgesic benefit; however, evidence is limited and heterogeneous. Conclusions TN may be understood as a disorder involving interactions between peripheral pathology and central nervous system reorganization. Integrating neuroimaging and molecular evidence may inform future patient stratification and neurosurgical decision-making. Individualized neuromodulation remains investigational and requires further clinical validation.

item.title: Impact of clinical risk factors on white matter microstructure in preterm-born infants: investigation with diffusion MRI and tractography at term-equivalent age.
item.description:
Journal of neural transmission (Vienna, Austria : 1996)
Premature birth occurs during a phase of intense brain maturation, making white matter (WM) particularly vulnerable to injury. Beyond major lesions, subtle and widespread microstructural alterations also contribute to later neurodevelopmental impairments. We aimed to characterize the impact of key clinical risk factors on global and tract-specific WM microstructure at term-equivalent age (TEA), using 3T-diffusion-MRI data of 111 infants born before 33 weeks of gestation. We implemented a tractography pipeline adapted for use in infants with heterogeneous brain anatomy, including macroscopic abnormalities and lesions, and extracted diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics in sensorimotor tracts: corticospinal tract (CST), superior thalamic radiation (STR), frontal aslant tract (FAT), forceps minor (FMI) and middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP). Associations with risk factors were assessed accounting for age at MRI or global WM microstructure. Tractography succeeded in most infants despite marked anatomical variability and/or overt lesions. Being a male, small for gestational age (SGA) at birth, encountering sepsis and having severe Kidokoro radiological score for WM were associated with altered global WM metrics. At the tract level, CST and STR showed the strongest susceptibility to SGA, prolonged parenteral nutrition, and Kidokoro score. In contrast, associations after adjustment for global WM microstructure suggested that FAT might be less vulnerable than other tracts to extreme prematurity, SGA and invasive ventilation. Findings were partially replicated in infants without macroscopic abnormalities, supporting the presence of WM dysmaturation even in the absence of visible injury. DTI metrics thus provide tract-specific biomarkers of early WM microstructure in preterm infants, which are sensitive to risk factors and could inform targeted prevention and intervention.

item.title: Mapping the topographic organization of the human zona incerta using diffusion MRI.
item.description:
eLife
The zona incerta (ZI) is a deep brain region originally described by Auguste Forel as an 'immensely confusing area about which nothing can be said'. Despite the elusive nature of this structure, mounting evidence supports the role of the ZI and surrounding regions across a diverse range of brain functions and as a candidate target for neuromodulatory therapies. Using in vivo diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and data-driven connectivity, we identify a topographic organization between the ZI and neocortex. Specifically, our methods identify a rostral-caudal gradient predominantly connecting the frontopolar and ventral prefrontal cortices with the rostral ZI, and the primary sensorimotor cortices with the caudal ZI. Moreover, we demonstrate how clustering and gradient approaches build complementary evidence including facilitating the mapping of a central region of the ZI, connected with the dorsal prefrontal cortex. These results were shown to be replicable across multiple datasets and at the individual subject level, building evidence for the important role of the ZI in mediating frontal lobe-associated tasks, ranging from motor to cognitive to emotional control. Finally, we consider the impact of this topographic organization on the refinement of neuromodulatory targets. These results pave the way for an increasingly detailed understanding of ZI substructures, and considerations for in vivo targeting of the ZI for neuromodulation.

item.title: Pediatric brain charts reveal ADHD biotypes with distinct developmental, molecular, and therapeutic profiles
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibits profound clinical heterogeneity; however, its underlying neurobiological substrates remain unclear. Here, leveraging large – scale structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 12,663 typically developing children and 1,699 children with ADHD across Chinese and United States cohorts, we construct population specific pediatric brain charts via hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling to quantify individual deviations in cortical morphology. Data-driven clustering identifies two robust, cross – ethnically replicable ADHD biotypes: an infra – normal biotype characterized by widespread cortical thinning and a supra – normal biotype marked by cortical thickening. Multivariate analyses reveal distinct brain–behavior architectures: cortical deviations correlate preferentially with symptom severity in the infra–normal biotype but with both symptom severity and cognitive performance in the supranormal biotype. Clinically, the infra–normal biotype demonstrates a superior response to methylphenidate over atomoxetine, whereas the supra–normal biotype responds comparably to both. Transcriptomic analyses identify biotype–specific molecular signatures converging with ADHD genome–wide association study (GWAS) risk loci but exhibiting distinct expression patterns in the brain. These findings classify ADHD heterogeneity into neurobiologically distinct, clinically informed biotypes, providing a mechanistic framework for precision psychiatry in pediatric ADHD.

item.title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. Methods: We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. Results: ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). Discussion: These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

item.title: Neuroanatomy of Orthorexia Nervosa: Emerging Insights from Structural Neuroimaging
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Objective There are no published studies in the contemporary scientific literature that have directly applied neuroimaging techniques (such as fMRI, PET, or structural/functional MRI) to individuals with orthorexia nervosa (ON) to characterize brain alterations specific to this condition. Although interest in ON is increasing, a critical area of investigation concerns its phenomenological overlap with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and other feeding and eating disorders (FED). The present study aims to examine morphological brain differences in individuals with ON using high-resolution 3D T1-weighted MRI, with the goal of determining whether structural profiles observed in ON are comparable to those seen in OCD and in established eating disorder phenotypes. Methods Twenty-seven participants (12 females, 15 males) were enrolled in the study and underwent a comprehensive psychometric assessment including the ORTO-15, Italian-Düsseldorf Orthorexia Scale (I-DOS), Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS), and the Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (MPS). Participants were stratified into those exhibiting orthorexic behaviour and those without (healthy control group, HC) according to ORTO-15 scores. The imaging protocol included the acquisition of high-resolution three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI scans. Groups were compared regarding cortical and subcortical parameters in order to identify neuroanatomical differences associated with orthorexic behaviour. Results Morphometric analysis revealed a significant correlation between ORTO-15 score and cortical thickness (CT) in key brain regions. Specifically, lower ORTO-15 scores—indicative of greater orthorexic tendencies—were associated with a marked reduction in CT of the entorhinal cortex (EC). Conversely, an increased CT was observed in the right posterior cingulate cortex (PCC). Discussions The observed alterations in the EC and PCC suggest that ON may share neurobiological patterns with OCD and FED. These findings support the notion of ON as a distinct yet transdiagnostic clinical entity. However, the small sample size highlights the need for further large-scale investigations to confirm the presence and reliability of these potential neurobiological biomarkers.

item.title: Changes in gray matter volume associated with gait speed and muscle mass in older adults with mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundMild cognitive impairment (MCI) is an early stage of cognitive decline between normal aging and dementia. Gait speed, a key marker of physical function, has been associated with both cognitive decline and brain atrophy. Sarcopenia, characterized by age-related loss of muscle mass and function, has also been linked to structural brain changes.ObjectiveTo investigate the associations between sarcopenia, its individual components and regional gray matter volume (GMV) in older adults with MCI.MethodsThis cross-sectional study included 234 older adults with MCI. Sarcopenia, gait speed, handgrip strength, and appendicular skeletal muscle mass index (ASMI) were assessed according to the 2019 Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia criteria. Brain T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging was analyzed using voxel-based morphometry. Voxel-wise group comparisons were performed to identify GMV differences after adjustment age, sex, comorbidity, depressive symptoms, nutritional status, and total intracranial volume.ResultsSlower gait speed was significantly associated with lower GMV in the bilateral putamen and left superior frontal cortex. Lower ASMI was associated with higher GMV in the left inferior temporal cortex. No significant GMV differences were found by sarcopenia status or handgrip strength.ConclusionsSlower gait speed is associated with reduced GMV in motor-related brain regions, indicating early brain structural changes in older adults with MCI. Although lower ASMI was associated with higher GMV, this finding should be interpreted cautiously. These findings highlight the complex interactions between physical function and brain structure, emphasizing gait speed as a potential indicator of brain health in older adults with MCI.

item.title: The uncinate fasciculus in frontotemporal dementia subtypes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of diffusion-tensor imaging studies.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundFrontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a leading cause of early-onset neurodegeneration with selective frontal and temporal lobe degeneration. Despite well-characterized gray and white matter atrophy patterns across FTD subtypes, the extent of degeneration of the uncinate fasciculus (UF) tract has not been systematically quantified across FTD subtypes.ObjectiveTo compare uncinate fasciculus fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, radial diffusivity, and axial diffusivity between frontotemporal dementia subtypes and healthy controls.MethodsWe systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of diffusion tensor imaging studies published between 2011 and October 2025 according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines.ResultsWe systematically reviewed 11 studies and performed a meta-analysis of 540 participants across 10 studies. We found that all FTD subtypes demonstrated significant degeneration of the UF compared to controls. The greatest effect sizes were observed when comparing the left UF between the semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA) and controls (FA: SMD = -2.5396, 95% CI: -3.7914, -1.2878, p < 0.0001; RD: SMD = 2.2414, 95% CI:1.7972, 2.6855, p < 0.0001; AD: SMD = 1.9831, 95% CI: 1.1434, 2.8227, p < 0.0001; MD: SMD = 2.5268, 95% CI: 1.9993, 3.0542, p < 0.0001), while the behavioral variant (bvFTD) showed the largest reduction in right UF fractional anisotropy. Within-group analyses revealed significant left-right asymmetry in svPPA and non-fluent aphasia (nfvPPA), with greater left UF involvement, while bvFTD and controls showed no hemispheric differences.ConclusionsWe highlight the UF as a promising tract for understanding disease mechanisms and developing imaging biomarkers in FTD.

item.title: An exploratory synthetic MRI-derived FLAIR-DIR contrast in olfactory-limbic regions in mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundOdor identification impairment is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease and predicts memory decline, but its microstructural basis remains unclear.ObjectiveTo evaluate FD, a semi-quantitative synthetic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR)-Double Inversion Recovery (DIR) contrast, against myelin volume fraction (MVF) in olfactory-limbic brain regions of patients diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI).MethodsSixteen healthy controls (HC) and 17 individuals diagnosed with MCI completed olfactory and cognitive testing and underwent 3T MRI using a QALAS sequence. MVF maps were generated and FD was computed as (FLAIR - DIR)/FLAIR. Group differences were examined in olfactory-limbic gray matter and associated white-matter tracts, and voxel-wise regression assessed FD-odor identification associations, including models adjusted for voxel-wise MVF. Region of interest and voxel-wise analyses were exploratory and largely uncorrected for multiple comparisons.ResultsCompared with HC, MCI showed lower FD across olfactory-limbic gray matter and white-matter pathways, including hippocampus, amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex, thalamus and corpus callosum, whereas MVF differences were more limited. Better odor identification was associated with higher FD in hippocampal/parahippocampal regions and insula, persisting after MVF adjustment. MVF showed positive associations in the right parahippocampal gyrus, left thalamus and genu of the corpus callosum. In an exploratory secondary analysis reported in the Supplemental Material, FD-based classification exceeded chance but was not separable from age alone.ConclusionsFD is a semi-quantitative relaxation-contrast metric showing regional patterns partially distinct from MVF. These exploratory findings require replication in larger, demographically matched, biomarker-confirmed cohorts before FD can be regarded as a marker of early olfactory-limbic microstructural change in MCI.

item.title: Temporal lobe cortical thickness and cognition in paediatric cancer survivors previously treated with chemotherapy.
item.description:
British journal of haematology
Long-term neurocognitive outcomes in paediatric cancer survivors treated with chemotherapy remain incompletely characterized, particularly in relation to cortical structure. Prior neuroimaging studies have included limited representation of racial and ethnic minority survivors. We analysed temporal lobe cortical thickness and cognition in paediatric cancer survivors treated with chemotherapy (n = 21; 8-25 years post-chemotherapy; aged 15-34 years) and age-matched controls (n = 21). Cognition was assessed using National Institute of Health (NIH) Toolbox scores. Cortical thickness of nine bilateral temporal regions was derived from T1-weighted 3T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) using FreeSurfer. Group differences and brain-cognition associations were analysed using adjusted regression models with false discovery rate correction. Survivors scored lower on crystallized (p < 0.001), fluid (p = 0.013) and total cognition scores (p = 0.001). They showed reduced temporal lobe cortical thickness (2.62 ± 0.13 vs. 2.74 ± 0.11 mm; p = 0.001), with reductions in seven subregions. Greater thickness was associated with better cognitive performance in 10 of 27 associations, most prominently for crystallized cognition. Fully corrected T-score sensitivity analyses showed crystallized cognition remained lower in survivors (p = 0.044). Paediatric cancer survivors previously treated with chemotherapy showed reduced temporal lobe cortical thickness, which was associated with worse crystallized cognition, suggesting a potential structure-function association.

item.title: Distinct profiles of white matter diffusivity in obesity and bipolar disorders: An ENIGMA bipolar disorders study in 2166 individuals.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
Background Bipolar disorders (BD) are associated with a wide range of brain white matter abnormalities, but results vary across studies. This heterogeneity likely relates to effects of additional clinical/diagnostic variables, including medications and obesity, on white matter in BD. In this mega-analysis, we studied the links between relevant clinical variables and four diffusivity measures. Methods We obtained diffusion tensor imaging-derived fractional anisotropy (FA), mean, axial, and radial diffusivity (MD, AD, RD) values from 910 individuals with BD and 1256 healthy controls across 16 research sites in the ENIGMA-BD Working Group. We used principal component analysis to detect patterns of covariance across white matter tracts and studied associations between multivariate patterns of white matter alterations and demographic and clinical variables, including body mass index (BMI), medications, and diagnostic information, using mixed regression models. Results Higher BMI was associated with lower PC1 FA and higher PC1 RD; BD was associated with higher PC1 MD, while treatment with antiepileptic medications was associated with lower PC1 FA, higher PC1 MD, and PC1 RD. Conclusions We found FA and MD are weakly associated, providing complementary information, and there are unique associations between specific diffusivity measures and clinical predictors. Treatment with antiepileptics may inflate the statistical effects of BD on white matter. By using all diffusivity measures and accounting for additional clinical factors, we can gain new insights into brain correlates of severe mental illness.

item.title: The Visual Cortex and Beyond: Investigating Long-Term Cortical Plasticity Following Monocular Deprivation.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Aim To characterise short- and long-term plastic changes in cortical and subcortical structures induced by ultra-long (five-day) monocular deprivation (MD), and to assess the extent and regional specificity of structural changes and their reversibility following the restoration of binocular vision. Methods In this single-arm longitudinal study, 21 healthy adults underwent five structural MRI sessions: at baseline, during MD on days 1, 3 and 5, and after a seven-day recovery period (day 12). MD was induced by occluding the right eye with a translucent eye patch for five consecutive days. Grey matter volume (GMV) changes were analysed using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) for whole-brain effects and generalised estimating equations (GEE) to model temporal trajectories in predefined cortical and subcortical regions. Results Ultra-long MD induced dynamic GMV changes in primary and higher visual cortices, with exploratory changes also in subcortical and cerebellar structures. VBM showed cumulative volume increases in bilateral occipital cortex, including calcarine, lateral occipital and fusiform regions, and adjacent cerebellar lobules, peaking between days 3 and 5. Region-wise modelling resolved the temporal build-up of these changes across visual, subcortical and sensorimotor regions; after correction for multiple comparisons, a time-dependent effect remained in occipital and ventral occipito-temporal cortex (occipital pole, fusiform and calcarine cortex), converging with the voxel-wise result. Following binocular restoration, an exploratory GMV decrease was observed selectively in the left middle occipital gyrus, while an exploratory increase was observed in the left hippocampus, compatible with persistent plasticity in associative memory networks. Conclusion Prolonged sensory imbalance via ultra-long MD induces rapid, region-specific and possibly persistent GMV plasticity in the adult brain. These changes follow temporally stratified trajectories across visual, subcortical and integrative systems, consistent with models of homeostatic and hierarchical plasticity. Corrected evidence supports cumulative occipital plasticity during deprivation; whether the exploratory extra-visual and post-recovery changes reflect persistent adaptation requires confirmation. MD-based paradigms thus offer a controlled window on structural plasticity in both healthy individuals and clinical populations.

item.title: Translational evidence for habenula's role in human addiction: A scoping review.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Addiction is characterized by persistent substance use or engagement in behaviors despite adverse consequences and impaired control, but its expression varies substantially across individuals, substances, and severity. Within one influential neurocircuitry framework, addiction processes are organized into binge, withdrawal, and preoccupation stages. Preclinical research implicates the habenula across these processes but indicates that its contribution varies across drugs, subdivisions, and experimental models. Research on the human habenula in addiction remains fragmented, and the extent to which it converges with preclinical mechanisms is unclear. This scoping review synthesized evidence on the human habenula in addiction and examined its convergence with preclinical findings. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, databases and grey literature were searched in November 2025, with literature surveillance continued through April 2026. Human studies reported reduced fronto-habenula white-matter integrity, elevated habenula-striatal resting-state functional connectivity, withdrawal-related habenula-frontal connectivity, increased habenula blood flow during opioid withdrawal, altered task-evoked responses to reward and feedback, and nicotine-related genetic signals. By contrast, morphological studies found no consistent differences in habenula structure across addiction samples. Most human neuroimaging studies could not distinguish the medial and lateral habenula, limiting direct comparison with subdivision-specific preclinical mechanisms. Overall, across human and preclinical studies, the evidence does not support a unitary habenular alteration across addiction. Cross-species convergence was strongest for withdrawal-related activity, particularly for opioids, and for nicotine-related molecular mechanisms, but remained limited by differences in substances, circuits, measures, and paradigms. Future studies using subdivision-sensitive imaging and more comparable cross-species designs are needed.

item.title: Positive-affective and negative-cognitive brain-behavior axes in clinical high risk for psychosis.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Background Individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR) present with heterogeneous combinations of positive, negative, and affective symptoms, cognitive difficulties, and functional impairment. However, reproducible multivariate links between this multidomain phenotype and brain morphology remain limited. This study explored the multivariate brain-behavior associations in CHR using a data-driven approach. Methods Baseline data from 720 CHR participants from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership® Schizophrenia program (AMP® SCZ) were analyzed using sparse canonical correlation analysis to identify associations between 95 regional brain volumes and 28 behavioral variables indexing symptoms, cognition, and functioning. Generalizability was tested using leave-one-network-out cross-validation (PRoNET and PRESCIENT), and stability was assessed using bootstrapping and leave-one-site-out analyses. Associations with demographic, clinical and site-related variables were examined. Results Two brain-behavior dimensions generalized across networks. A positive-affective axis (r=0.21-0.23), linking higher depression, anxiety/stress, positive symptoms and anhedonia with predominantly frontal-cingulate-insular volume reductions and relatively larger corpus callosum and putamen volumes. This axis was associated with comorbid depression, cannabis use and family history of depression or affective psychosis. A negative-cognitive axis (r=0.17-0.18) linked greater asociality, alogia, emotional withdrawal, blunted affect, and motor retardation, poorer cognition and functioning with reduced cerebellar and parietal volumes, and relatively larger lateral ventricles and corpus callosum. This axis was associated with lower IQ and poorer premorbid adjustment. Conclusions Two partially dissociable brain-behavior dimensions were identified: a positive-affective axis capturing the co-expression of affective and attenuated positive symptoms, and a negative-cognitive axis suggestive of neurodevelopmental vulnerability.

item.title: The Spectrum within the Spectrum: Neural Heterogeneity in Autism.
item.description:
Behavioural brain research
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses diverse behavioral, cognitive, and neural profiles that vary widely across individuals. Because diagnosis remains predominantly behavior-based, clinically meaningful within-spectrum differences are often missed. Recent advances in neuroimaging analysis have created opportunities for the identification of distinct neural profiles within ASD. These new avenues provide ways to examine intra-ASD heterogeneity directly, identifying person-specific brain-behavior patterns that group-level comparisons fail to capture. The present systematic review focused on neuroimaging methods (i.e., resting-state fMRI; rs-fMRI, cortical morphology) that emphasized heterogeneity-informed outcomes based on normative modeling, data-driven subtyping, clustering analysis and similar analytic choices. For rs-fMRI, findings showed that differences in connectivity within the default mode and salience networks were linked to social-communication and language impairments, with subtype-specific patterns emerging across samples. In cortical thickness and surface area, studies identified distinct developmental trajectories and individual deviation profiles, with prefrontal and temporal regions often tied to repetitive behaviors and social-communication difficulties. Voxel-based analyses revealed subgroup-specific gray matter alterations, including cerebellar and cortical differences, that aligned with variation in repetitive behaviors and social difficulties. Collectively, this emerging evidence supports the notion that neural heterogeneity in autism is a core feature rather than a limitation. Embracing individual variability can provide crucial insight into the inconsistencies and contradictions of earlier case-control and group-level findings. Moving forward, autism research must prioritize heterogeneity-based methods to establish reproducible subtypes and individualized brain-behavior links.

item.title: Loneliness relates to smaller hippocampal subfield volumes in individuals with elevated plasma pTau217: results from IGNITE.
item.description:
GeroScience
Loneliness is associated with cognitive decline and dementia risk, but the role of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology in its associations with medial temporal lobe (MTL) morphology remains unclear. We examined whether loneliness was related to total hippocampal volume, hippocampal subfields, and entorhinal cortex (ERC) volumes, and whether plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (pTau217) moderated these relationships. We analyzed baseline data from cognitively unimpaired older adults aged 65-80 years enrolled in IGNITE. Loneliness was assessed using the revised UCLA Loneliness Scale. Structural 3 T MRI included a high-resolution T2-weighted hippocampal sequence. Hippocampal subfields and ERC volumes were extracted using ASHS, and FreeSurfer estimated total hippocampal volume and intracranial volume. Participants were classified as pTau217-positive or negative using an Aβ-PET-calibrated threshold (> 0.46 pg/mL). Covariate-adjusted linear regression models tested loneliness associations and loneliness×pTau217 interactions. We included 601 participants (69.8 ± 3.7 years; 72.2% female; 76.4% White); 582 had usable pTau217 data, of whom 28.9% were pTau217-positive. pTau217 moderated associations with CA3 (β = - 0.215, 95% CI - 0.381 to - 0.048) and ERC (β = - 0.167, 95% CI - 0.318 to - 0.016), with negative associations observed among pTau217-positive but not pTau217-negative participants. Greater loneliness was associated with smaller total hippocampal volume (β = - 0.077, 95% CI, - 0.147 to - 0.007, p = 0.031), but not with individual subfields. Loneliness showed biomarker-dependent associations with MTL subfields, suggesting that pTau217-defined biological risk may modify links between psychosocial factors and neuroanatomical vulnerability. This biomarker-informed framework may help explain heterogeneity in prior loneliness-neuroimaging findings.Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02875301.

item.title: HD-DRUM Rhythmic Training in Huntington's Disease: Feasibility, Motor, and Brain Microstructural Pilot Signals.
item.description:
Movement disorders clinical practice
Background Rhythmic cuing may benefit motor functions in Huntington's disease (HD) by compensating for the loss of predictive timing associated with basal ganglia degeneration. To our knowledge no remote rhythmic training application has been developed or evaluated that seeks to improve function in HD. HD-DRUM is a tablet-based rhythmic cuing application for the training of paced movements. Feasibility of 8 weeks at-home HD-DRUM compared with usual-activity control was assessed in a two-arm, pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) in people with HD. HD-DRUM-related changes in motor and cognitive functions, mood, and brain microstructure were explored. Objectives Primary outcomes were feasibility rates (recruitment, retention, adherence, acceptability) for an effectiveness RCT. Secondary outcomes were estimates of HD-DRUM-related effect sizes on motor functions, cognition, mood, and brain microstructure to explore training mechanisms. Methods Fifty-five individuals with HD were randomized into either HD-DRUM (n = 32, 1 excluded) or control (n = 23) groups. Participants underwent Quantitative-Motor, cognitive and mood assessments and diffusion-weighted MRI at baseline and follow-up. Recruitment, retention, and adherence rates were recorded, and HD-DRUM acceptability was assessed with a self-report questionnaire. Group differences of changes in behavioral and brain microstructural measures were reported with 95% confidence intervals. Results Acceptability of HD-DRUM, retention, and adherence rates averages were high (>80%) and target recruitment was reached. Performance in paced tapping and brain microstructure in motor networks signaled training benefits and were associated with each other. Conclusions HD-DRUM may provide an accessible intervention that can aid maintenance of motor function and brain microstructure in HD.

item.title: A brain–behavior generative model links individual brain dynamics to perceptual decisions
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Perceptual decision speed varies across individuals and trials. Explaining this variability requires linking individual brain anatomy, neural dynamics, and behavior, yet whole-brain models typically reproduce brain signals without behavior, whereas behavioral models lack anatomical constraints. Here we introduce a brain–behavior generative model in which whole-brain dynamics on each participant’s structural connectome generate both single-trial electroencephalography (EEG) and reaction times. Fitted to 17 participants performing motion discrimination, the models reproduced individual eventrelated potentials and reaction-time distributions. Joint fitting enabled the models to predict whether held-out trials were relatively fast or slow within each stimulus condition. In silico silencing further predicted where, how, and when each person’s brain controls decision speed. Sensorimotor regions affected decision speed consistently across most participants, whereas the same parietal region had opposite effects in different participants. These opposite effects reflected whether the region acted mainly through network dynamics or the decision readout. Temporal analyses suggested that early activity largely set decision speed, whereas late EEG mainly tracked the unfolding decision. These results show that brain–behavior generative modeling can link individual brain dynamics to perceptual decisions and yield testable predictions of why decision speed varies across individuals and trials.

item.title: Field Position and Subjective Number of Headers Are Associated with Subcortical Volumes in Female Soccer Players.
item.description:
AJNR. American journal of neuroradiology
Background and purpose Repetitive head impacts (RHI) from soccer headers could be linked to neurodegeneration, but their effects on young, active athletes are still under debate. This exploratory, cross-sectional study aimed to generate hypotheses about the relationship between soccer headers, brain volume alterations, and neuropsychological function in female soccer players. The analysis focused on brain regions previously identified as vulnerable to RHI. Materials and methods Nineteen semiprofessional female soccer players (mean age: 22.4 ± 4.1 years) and 15 noncontact-sport controls underwent structural MRI. Players were assessed for neuropsychological function and measures of exposure (field position, subjective number of headers, age at first exposure, and total years played). Subcortical gray and corpus callosum white matter volumes were calculated using FreeSurfer for all participants. Group differences in brain volumes were assessed. Among players, associations between brain volumes, exposure measures, and neuropsychological function were analyzed, controlling for multiple comparisons using a 25% false discovery rate. Results This study found no statistically significant group differences in brain regional volumes. Among players, a higher subjective number of headers correlated with lower left thalamic (r = -0.54; P = .02) and posterior corpus callosum volumes (r = -0.57; P = .01), whereas field positions with an expected higher number of headers were linked to lower volumes of the right nucleus accumbens (r = 0.58; P = .01) and hippocampus (r = 0.72; P = .001). No statistically significant associations were found for other exposure measures, brain volumes, or any of the neuropsychological outcomes. Conclusions A higher subjective number of headers among female soccer players was associated with group-level findings regarding reduced subcortical gray and central white matter brain volumes in our small sample of female soccer players. Although these findings are exploratory, group level, and of uncertain clinical significance, they provide hypotheses for future studies and suggest directions for further investigation.

item.title: DTI-Associated Blood Biomarkers in a Human Perioperative Brain Perturbation Model.
item.description:
Journal of neurotrauma
Circulating biomarkers of brain perturbation are rarely evaluated against anatomically localized in vivo imaging measures, limiting biological interpretation. We tested whether perioperative changes in candidate biomarkers were associated with diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)-defined microstructural changes in a controlled human perioperative model. In a paired cohort of 75 patients undergoing left-sided encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis, we obtained matched pre- and postoperative DTI and blood samples. Six biomarkers (ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase-L1 [UCH-L1], glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP], S100 calcium-binding protein B [S100B], neurofilament light chain, neuron-specific enolase, and protein tau) were quantified. Analyses included paired comparisons, region-of-interest-based cross-modal correlations, sparse canonical correlation analysis (sCCA) with bootstrap stability assessment, and patient-grouped regularized logistic regression for state discrimination. DTI showed perioperative changes in bilateral temporal-limbic regions and connected white matter, with the largest effects in left hippocampal and amygdalar territories on the operated side. UCH-L1, GFAP, and S100B showed the clearest paired increases and dominated internal perioperative-state discrimination. Blood-DTI associations were heterogeneous across biomarkers and states, and paired-change associations were not confined to these three markers. An observed three-biomarker panel discriminated perioperative state with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.914 in the test set. Several circulating biomarkers covaried with regional DTI measures in this exploratory perioperative cohort. UCH-L1, GFAP, and S100B were the most perioperatively responsive and state-discriminative markers, but the DTI-association pattern was not specific to this trio. The findings support a structure-associated framework for evaluating blood biomarkers against regional imaging changes; they do not validate these biomarkers for traumatic brain injury, and relevance to traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains hypothesis-generating.

item.title: Longitudinal Changes in Brain Connectivity and Structure after MRgFUS VIM Thalamotomy for Essential Tremor.
item.description:
Stereotactic and functional neurosurgery
Essential Tremor (ET) is the most common movement disorder. Magnetic Resonance-guided Focused Ultrasound (MRgFUS), an incisionless surgery involving thermal ablation of targeted brain regions, like the Ventral Intermediate Nucleus of the Thalamus (VIM) and surrounding white matter tracts, is an effective treatment option. Fractional Anisotropy (FA), a metric of diffusion tensor imaging, can be used to determine white matter structural integrity and their changes following MRgFUS. This study investigates white matter and morphological brain remodeling after MRgFUS VIM thalamotomy and its association with tremor improvement, assessed by the Clinical Rating Scale for Tremor (CRST), over the first postoperative year. We retrospectively analyzed 56 ET patients who underwent unilateral MRgFUS VIM thalamotomy. Subjects' CRST scores, T1-weighted MRI scans, and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) scans were acquired pre-operatively and at three and twelve months post-operatively. FA maps were generated and registered to a standard space. Voxel clusters that exhibited significant change in FA over time were identified using FSL's cluster tool (p<0.001) and their change in FA value over time was Spearman correlated with relative change in CRST score. Deformation-Based Morphometry of T1-weighted images evaluated changes in structural volume, and a linear mixed-effects model was applied. We permuted these values 1000 times randomly to isolate significant (p<0.01) clusters related to the interaction between time and outcome and Spearman correlated them with relative improvement in CRST. Four main FA clusters demonstrated strong associations between CRST score and time. The insula produced consistent positive correlations at three (R=0.32, p=0.04) and twelve months (R=0.29, p=0.11). Yet, the visual cortex exhibited no significant association at three months (R=0.11, p=0.46), but did at twelve months (R=0.35, p=0.05), suggesting malleable white matter remodeling. Our morphometry analysis revealed two primary clusters located in the pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA) and visual cortex. The pre-SMA exhibited the strongest correlations at three months (three months: R=0.34, p=0.03, twelve months: R=0.17, p=0.36), while the visual cortex displayed a similar strength throughout (three months: R=0.20, p=0.18, twelve months: R=-0.22, p=0.23). These findings suggest that MRgFUS VIM thalamotomy is associated with broad structural tract and volumetric changes that extend beyond motor networks. Both analyses demonstrated post-treatment volume growth and increased tract structure in visual and cognitive regions. Correlation with tremor improvement indicates many of these changes may contribute to individual outcomes during the first post-operative year.

item.title: Gray matter volume is associated with pain and masticatory performance in temporomandibular disorders-related myalgia: A longitudinal MRI study.
item.description:
Cranio : the journal of craniomandibular practice
Objective Neuroimaging evidence has increasingly revealed associations between brain mechanisms and temporomandibular disorders (TMD). However, current cross-sectional findings have not elucidated the neural mechanisms underlying dynamic changes in pain and mastication. This longitudinal study investigated gray matter volume (GMV) of the brain in patients with TMD-related myalgia and its associations with pain intensity and masticatory performance. Methods Twenty-one TMD patients were investigated for current pain, muscle pain, and masticatory performance before (T0 ) and after (T1 ) treatment. Among the patients, 13 received structural magnetic resonance imaging. GMV was compared between TMD patients and matched non-TMD controls, and the association between GMV at T0 and clinical variables was investigated in TMD patients. Results Between the TMD and non-TMD groups, no significant GMV differences were found. However, total GMV was significantly lower in T1 compared to T0 . Greater T0 GMV in the superior frontal gyrus and primary motor cortex was associated with greater current pain and better masticatory performance at T0 , respectively. Greater T0 GMV in the anterior insula was associated with a lower muscle pain score at T1 . Conclusion The new findings suggest that individual differences in structural brain features may be associated with pain and masticatory performance before and after TMD treatment.

item.title: Neonatal brain network integration trajectories predict neurodevelopment in congenital heart disease.
item.description:
Pediatric research
Background Infants with critical congenital heart disease (CHD) are at high risk for abnormal brain development and later neurodevelopmental impairment. We hypothesized that the trajectory of perioperative whole-brain network development would predict neurodevelopmental outcomes in early childhood. Methods This prospective longitudinal cohort of neonates with critical CHD (n = 97) underwent preoperative and/or postoperative brain MRI with diffusion imaging. Whole-brain network measures were derived from structural connectomes from 80 infants, and 50 had neurodevelopment assessed at 1-4 years using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development. Results White matter injury was associated with a slower perioperative increase in global efficiency (p = 0.013), a measure of network integration, whereas cardiac physiology was not associated with network development. Infants with greater perioperative increases in global efficiency had higher cognitive (p = 0.001), language (p < 0.001), and motor (p = 0.008) scores. For each 1-standard deviation increase in the trajectory of global efficiency, cognitive scores increased by 8.2 points (95% CI: 3.64-12.78), independent of brain injury and socioeconomic factors. Conclusion In infants with critical CHD, longitudinal whole-brain network development was associated with neurodevelopment across multiple domains. Early network development may serve as a biomarker of neurodevelopmental risk and resilience in this population. Impact In infants with critical congenital heart disease, perioperative increase in whole-brain network integration was associated with cognitive, language, and motor outcomes in early childhood. White matter injury was associated with a slower increase in network integration, whereas cardiac physiology subtype was not associated with network development. This study extends prior work by showing that a longitudinal measure of neonatal whole-brain network development, rather than a single imaging timepoint, predicts neurodevelopment across multiple domains. These findings identify early network development as a potential biomarker of neurodevelopmental risk and resilience, and support future risk-stratification and intervention studies in this population.

item.title: Structural brain correlates of symptom severity in stress-induced exhaustion.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Exhaustion due to chronic stress, a hallmark feature of burnout, represents a substantial and growing public health burden, yet its structural brain correlates remain poorly understood. We used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to examine associations between regional gray matter volume and symptom severity in a cohort of 300 individuals on self-reported sick leave due to the Swedish medical condition stress-induced exhaustion disorder (ED), characterized by debilitating fatigue following prolonged stress exposure. Symptom severity was assessed using the Shirom-Melamed Burnout Questionnaire (SMBQ-18) and its subscales. Overall symptom severity (SMBQ-18 total score) and Physical Exhaustion (PE) were negatively associated with gray matter volume in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a region implicated in stress regulation and affective control, which remained significant when adjusting for depressive symptoms. An exploratory finding was that Listlessness was negatively associated with gray matter volume in the bilateral hippocampi and right middle temporal gyrus after adjustment for depressive symptoms. These results provide evidence from a large cohort for brain-symptom associations in chronic stress and highlight the value of dimensional approaches for capturing heterogeneity in stress-related conditions.

item.title: Advanced brain age and longitudinal cognitive decline in healthy older adults.
item.description:
GeroScience
Advanced brain age relative to chronological age may predict cognitive decline in healthy aging, but prospective evidence remains limited. We tested whether the brain age gap (BAG) predicts cognition and 5-year cognitive decline in the AGES-Reykjavik Study. Participants with structural MRI and neuropsychological data were included cross-sectionally (n = 4,606); mean age 76.4y; 58% female) and longitudinally (n = 2,561; mean follow-up 5.2y). BAG was estimated from T1-weighted MRI. Mixed-effects models examined BAG effects on Memory (M), processing speed (PS), and executive function (EF), adjusting for age, sex, and education. Higher BAG was associated with worse cognition across all domains (β = -0.037 to -0.047, all p < 0.001). BAG significantly predicted greater decline in M (β = -0.007, p = 0.046); subgroup analyses revealed steeper decline in M and EF with advanced brain age. BAG predicts longitudinal cognitive decline beyond chronological age, supporting its utility as a biomarker in preventative care of healthy aging.

item.title: Glymphatic dysfunction in early-onset schizophrenia: DTI-ALPS index reduction tracks illness burden and is independently associated with cognitive performance in treatment-resistant patients.
item.description:
European child & adolescent psychiatry
Early-onset schizophrenia (EOS) is associated with greater cognitive impairment than adult-onset disease, and many patients also develop treatment resistance. Glymphatic dysfunction has been described in adult schizophrenia but not in EOS or in relation to treatment resistance. We used diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) to assess glymphatic function in 30 adolescents with EOS (15 treatment-resistant, TRS; 15 non-treatment-resistant, nTRS) and 29 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC). Participants completed a neuropsychological battery covering verbal memory, processing speed, executive function, working memory, verbal fluency, and social cognition. ALPS differed across groups (F(2,56) = 34.66, p < 0.001, η² = 0.553), with values decreasing from HC (1.625 ± 0.072) to nTRS (1.501 ± 0.098) to TRS (1.439 ± 0.048); the TRS-nTRS difference was not significant (d = 0.81, p = 0.066). Patients showed broad cognitive deficits relative to HC, but nTRS and TRS did not differ on any measure after FDR correction. ALPS showed a nominal inverse association with the number of psychotic episodes (ρ = -0.391, p = 0.033) but was unrelated to PANSS scores or antipsychotic dose. Within TRS, ALPS was independently associated with phonemic verbal fluency (COWAT: β = +0.74, p = 0.003); a parallel association with categorical fluency (β = +0.88, p < 0.001) was partly driven by an influential observation and is exploratory. Glymphatic dysfunction appears to be a disease-intrinsic feature of EOS, lowest in TRS, possibly linked to cumulative episodes rather than current symptoms, and may contribute to cognitive impairment in treatment-resistant patients.

item.title: Quantifying dexterity and grip strength associations between age, cognitive function (MoCA), and cerebellar gray matter volume in healthy adults across the adult lifespan.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Cerebellar Crus I/II gray matter volume (GMV) is a structural marker of cognitive aging, and motor performance predicts age-related cognitive decline. Whether grip strength and manual dexterity dissociate in their cerebellar and cognitive correlates is unknown. We computed Pearson partial correlations (age, sex, and race covaried) between grip strength, Nine-Hole Peg Test (9HPT) dexterity, cerebellar Crus I/II GMV, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) subscores in 304 healthy adults aged 20-79 from the University of South Carolina Aging Brain Cohort. GMV was derived from T1-weighted MRI using CAT12 with the AAL3 atlas. After false discovery rate (FDR) correction, dominant 9HPT time correlated with MoCA total score (r=-.240) and memory index (r=-.220; both pFDR<0.001). Grip strength was unrelated to any MoCA measure but correlated bilaterally with Crus II GMV (r=.156-.224, all pFDR≤0.041). Bootstrapped mediation indicated that dexterity statistically accounted for 28.8% of the age-cognition association and Crus II volume for 34.4-41.4% of the age-grip association. Dichotomizing at the MoCA cut-off of 26, each additional second of peg time carried 17.6% higher odds of scoring below cut-off (odds ratio = 1.176, 95% CI [1.062,1.302]) while grip strength carried none. Grip strength, but not dexterity, was independently associated with Crus II GMV, whereas dexterity, but not grip, was associated with cognition. Grip strength and dexterity are therefore not interchangeable indices of motor function. Because the design is cross-sectional, mediation estimates describe shared variance rather than causal pathways, and the pronounced MoCA ceiling likely attenuated the cognitive associations.

item.title: Anatomically optimised structural connectome derivation for the neonatal brain
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Structural connectomics provides a means of characterising white matter (WM) network organisation using diffusion MRI (dMRI), but reconstructing neonatal structural connectomes remains challenging due to the immature and heterogeneous nature of the developing brain. Although recent neonatal studies have increasingly adopted approaches beyond conventional diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), there remains scope to incorporate more advanced tractography and streamline post-processing approaches within neonatal pipelines. Here, we propose a neonatal structural connectome pipeline integrating surface-based anatomical constraints, ensemble tractography, hierarchical anatomical refinement of pathways (HARP) filtering, and spherical-deconvolution informed filtering (SIFT2) reweighting. We acquired 3T MRI data from 300 neonates (185 preterm, 115 term-born) to assess the impact of pipeline configuration on network organisation. Mean gestational age (GA) at birth was 29.31 (23.43–32.86) weeks in preterm infants and 39.52 (37.00–42.43) weeks in term infants. At scan, mean GA was 40.85 (36.29–49.00) weeks in preterm infants and 42.06 (38.29–48.00) weeks in term infants. Four connectome variants were generated: raw surfaced-based tractograms, HARP-filtered, SIFT2-weighted, and combined HARP+SIFT2. Pipeline performance was primarily evaluated using an existing brain age prediction model: connectome-based predictive model (CPM) and our derived connectomes to estimate GA at scan in term and preterm infants. In addition, global graph theoretical metric analyses were conducted to provide a complementary assessment of pipeline configuration differences in network organisation. In total, seven graph theoretical metrics were calculated and evaluated: global efficiency, local efficiency, transitivity, modularity, assortativity, degree variance and statistical complexity. Across all configurations, connectomes supported accurate brain age prediction, with mean absolute errors (MAE) of 0.76–0.79 weeks in term infants and 1.00–1.06 weeks in preterm infants. Prediction error and brain age gap variability were greater in preterm than term infants across configurations, with HARP+SIFT2 achieving the lowest preterm MAE (1.00 weeks) and brain age gap (BAG) variability (SD = 1.38 weeks). However, differences in prediction performance across configurations were minimal, suggesting limited influence of pipeline choice on brain age prediction.
