However, analysis of global network metrics demonstrated that pipeline choice significantly influenced downstream measures of network organisation, with HARP+SIFT2 being the only configuration to identify significant preterm vs. term differences across all seven metrics examined. These findings demonstrate the importance of considering tractography and streamline-processing choices when constructing neonatal structural connectomes and provide a framework for more anatomically informed investigation of early brain development. item.title: Dose-dependent myelin g-ratio alterations in the white matter of 16p11.2 copy number variations
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Copy number variations (CNVs) at the 16p11.2 locus are major genetic risk factors for neurodevelopmental conditions and drive reciprocal alterations in cerebral white matter structure and connectivity. However, whether these alterations reflect differences in the axonal or myelin compartments remains unresolved with conventional diffusion MRI. We combined diffusion MRI with magnetization transfer saturation mapping across two ComBat-harmonized cohorts comprising 80 controls, 26 16p11.2 deletion carriers, and 13 duplication carriers. We quantified axonal volume, myelin volume, and aggregate g-ratio of white matter tracts forming the structural connectome. Metrics were evaluated using normative modeling across tract length, resting-state functional networks, and cortical nodes. We additionally examined 29 individuals carrying other neurodevelopmental CNVs. 16p11.2 gene dosage was associated with regional reciprocal differences in tract axonal volume, with greater volume in deletion carriers and lower volume in duplication carriers. In contrast, myelin volume did not differ significantly from controls. This mismatch resulted in pervasive aggregate g-ratio alterations, with higher g-ratios (relatively thinner myelin sheaths) in deletion carriers and lower g-ratios (relatively thicker sheaths) in duplication carriers. Regional g-ratio alterations also extended to other neurodevelopmental CNVs. These findings resolve some of the biological ambiguity underlying white matter alterations in 16p11.2 CNV carriers, implicating the axonal compartment while revealing comparatively stable myelin volume. The disrupted axon-myelin scaling results in connectome-wide g-ratio alterations and may represent a shared microstructural hallmark of genetic neurodevelopmental risk.

item.title: Perisynaptic matrix gene variants underlie DystoniaGeneNet endophenotypes in isolated focal dystonia
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Isolated focal dystonia is a rare movement disorder characterized by abnormalities in brain structure and function. The genes underlying isolated focal dystonia are not fully elucidated, and genetic studies are constrained by incomplete penetrance and small family sizes. Neuroimaging endophenotypes shared by patients and unaffected relatives can reveal genetic liability independently of clinical manifestation and offer a strategy for advancing gene discovery. We developed DystoniaGeneNet, a 3D convolutional neural network that predicts familial status from T1-weighted brain MRIs. We then used its predictions to guide genetic analyses in isolated focal dystonia. DystoniaGeneNet was trained on 40 patients with familial laryngeal dystonia and 40 healthy controls, then applied to independent cohorts of 21 patients with familial isolated focal dystonia, 364 patients with sporadic dystonia, and 98 unaffected relatives. Model predictions were incorporated into variant prioritization and segregation analysis in 214 individuals with whole-exome sequencing data, and results were replicated in another 738 independent exomes, in genetic data from a hospital-based biobank (892 dystonia cases, 2,475 controls), and in the All of Us Research Program genetic data (1,343 dystonia cases, 6,840 controls). DystoniaGeneNet discriminated familial dystonia from healthy controls in the training set and correctly classified 85.7% of independent familial cases, using a biomarker centred on the corpus callosum and inferior temporal gyrus. Across the discovery and replication cohorts, we identified rare, likely pathogenic genetic variants in RAP1GAP and TNN segregating with disease in families. Additional variants were found in singletons with isolated focal dystonia. In patients with clinically sporadic dystonia but predicted to have familial features, we observed multiple rare variants in ITSN2 , including three high-confidence loss-of-function variants, and an enrichment of damaging missense variants in its Dbl homology domain. To determine the functional impact of discovered genetic variants, we assessed gene expression and splicing via qPCR and RNA sequencing ( n = 74), revealing reduced RAP1GAP and ITSN2 expression in variant carriers. At the pathway level, rare nonsynonymous variants in brain-expressed matrisome genes were associated with dystonia ( P = 0.012). Our strategy utilizing a deep learning-derived neuroimaging endophenotype to empower gene discovery uncovered RAP1GAP, TNN , and ITSN2 as novel genes associated with isolated focal dystonia. These genes converge on perisynaptic extracellular matrix-synapse signalling, implicating a mechanism linked to synaptic plasticity deficits, and identifying a molecular substrate for network-level brain abnormalities that characterize this disorder. Further, we exemplify a generalizable framework for leveraging endophenotypes in rare neurogenetic diseases with incomplete penetrance.

item.title: Age and sex differences in T1 relaxation times and volumetrics in segmented brain and upper cervical spine in healthy participants using MP2RAGE protocol at 3.0 T.
item.description:
AJNR. American journal of neuroradiology
Background and purpose To examine the influence of age and sex on T1 relaxation and volume in brain and upper cervical cord using MP2RAGE, which offers high contrast-to-noise ratio, uniform tissue contrast, and superior anatomical resolution alongside T1 mapping. This provides an accurate analysis of the magnitude of the effects of these covariates on the outcomes. Materials and methods 208 MP2RAGE scans from the Max Planck Institute Leipzig Mind-Brain-Body LEMON dataset were segmented and labeled using FreeSurfer and Spinal Cord Toolbox. The influences of age and sex on dependent variables were analyzed using linear regression and group difference were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. Results T1 values of cortical gray matter (GM), cerebral white matter (WM), thalamus, caudate, putamen, hippocampus, amygdala, and anterior corpus callosum (CC) varied significantly with age. Cortical GM and cervical C1 T1 showed statistical significance with sex, with latter lower in the females compared to males. T1 values of the posterior CC were significantly lower than the anterior portion. GM, WM, thalamus, caudate, putamen, hippocampus and anterior CC volumes were significantly affected by age. Spine cross-sectional area (CSA) showed statistically significant differences with sex but not age. Conclusions T1, regional brain volumes, and spinal CSA vary according to anatomical location, age, and sex, reflecting physiological differences associated with aging and sex. These results can operate as a normative baseline to gauge the magnitude of effect of these covariates on future studies in health or disease.

item.title: The Association Between Cardiorespiratory Fitness and White Matter Integrity Across the Lifespan: A Systematic Review
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
White matter deterioration is a hallmark of cognitive aging and a core feature of manyneurodegenerative disorders. Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) has emerged as a modifiable factorthat may support white matter integrity across the adult lifespan. This systematic review, using anarrative synthesis, examined findings from 24 studies, identified through a systematic search ofPubMed, Web of Science, and PsycINFO databases, examining the association betweenobjectively measured CRF and neuroimaging-based white matter structure. Results revealed aconsistent positive relationship between higher CRF and stronger microstructural integrity,particularly in late-myelinating tracts such as the corpus callosum, cingulum, and longitudinalfasciculi. These associations were minimal in young adulthood, mixed in midlife, and mostrobust in adults over 60, suggesting an age-dependent neuroprotective effect that strengthensacross the lifespan. Higher CRF was also linked to reduced white matter hyperintensity (WMH)burden in older populations. While cross-sectional evidence for this relationship was largelyconsistent, findings from randomized controlled trials were considerably more mixed, with mostintervention studies failing to detect group-level improvements in white matter microstructuredespite confirmed fitness gains. These findings underscore the potential of CRF as a nonpharmacological strategy to preserve brain health and mitigate cognitive decline with age. Futureresearch should adopt longitudinal and multimodal designs to clarify causal mechanisms andidentify age-specific moderators of these effects. Keywords: cardiorespiratory fitness, white matter, fractional anisotropy, aging, aerobic exercise

item.title: The Influence of Contralesional Brain Age Gradients on Chronic Stroke Aphasia Severity and Treatment Response.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The adult brain follows normative aging trajectories, yet stroke abruptly disrupts this process. Beyond the focal lesion, undamaged regions can deviate from expected aging due to diaschisis or pre-existing vulnerabilities, reflecting tissue health that may constrain recovery. Chronic post-stroke aphasia, a persistent language disorder, shows wide individual variability in severity and treatment response, and these differences are not fully captured by lesion characteristics or demographic factors. Further, prior imaging biomarkers have been difficult to scale because they rely on specialized acquisitions or nonstandardized analytical pipelines. Here, we used a standardized, lifespan-informed brain age model (volBrain) trained on large public datasets to quantify regional deviations from normative aging using only routine structural MRI (T1-weighted). In 188 individuals with chronic stroke (67 female, 121 male), regional aging deviations in the contralesional hemisphere explained aphasia severity beyond lesion volume, lesion location, and basic demographics. In a treated subgroup, baseline brain aging patterns also predicted language gains that persisted 6 months after therapy, indicating prognostic value. By characterizing how individual brains diverge from expected aging, this approach captures variation in tissue integrity that is relevant for both impairment and recovery. This provides a scalable framework that can be integrated across sites and studies, linking normative aging models with post-stroke prognostics and informing precision neurorehabilitation.

item.title: Regional blood-brain barrier dysfunction maps to lower performance in cognitive ageing.
item.description:
Brain communications
Age-related cognitive decline is a common and growing public health challenge, associated with loss of independence, reduced quality of life, increased caregiver burden and substantial healthcare and societal costs. Yet cognitive decline in ageing is heterogeneous, and current clinical constructs do not reliably capture the underlying biological mechanisms or predict progression to dementia. This cross-sectional study examined whether blood-brain barrier dysfunction (BBBD) provides a biologically supported correlate of cognitive performance beyond clinical diagnosis. The study included 46 patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), 46 age-matched controls and 43 young controls. BBBD was assessed using dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI in 42 patients with MCI and all controls, alongside volumetric brain analysis. Standardized NeuroTrax cognitive assessment data were analysed for 41 MCI patients and 19 age-matched controls. BBBD was analysed using the BBBdetect software (Emagix Inc, Nova Scotia, Canada), quantifying voxelwise and region-wise blood-brain barrier permeability; volumetric analysis was performed using the Volbrain software; and cognitive performance was stratified into low- and high-performance subgroups based on modified z-scores. Compared with young controls, the older cohort (MCI patients combined with age-matched controls) showed significantly greater BBBD volume and regional extent. Permeability increased with age and showed marked inter-individual variability. Across participants, lower cognitive performance was associated with a greater number of regions exhibiting BBBD. Receiver operating characteristic analysis identified domain-specific spatial patterns of BBBD linked to poor performance in memory, executive, attention, verbal and motor domains, implicating frontal, cingulate, hippocampal, basal ganglia and cerebellar regions. In contrast, volumetric analyses revealed expected age-related reductions in grey and white matter and cortical thickness along with increased ventricular volume; however, these structural changes showed weak to no associations with cognitive performance. These findings suggest that BBBD is widespread in ageing and that regional BBBD maps to domain-specific cognitive deficits. BBBD thus emerges as a biologically relevant biomarker of age-related cognitive impairment and a potential therapeutic target for preserving cognitive function in ageing.

item.title: The mediating effect of circulating C-reactive protein on the association between depression and brain cortical dysconnectivity.
item.description:
Psychiatry research. Neuroimaging
Chronic low grade systemic inflammation is associated in the pathophysiology of major depressive disorder (MDD). However, the specific cortical structural connectivity changes associated with peripheral inflammation in MDD remains poorly understood. In this case-control study, 113 MDD patients and 107 healthy controls underwent 3T MRI and measurement of high sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP). Fiber connectivity density (FiCD) mapping, a data driven whole-cortex pipeline combining cortical surface reconstruction with diffusion tractography, was used to examine depression and CRP interaction effects on cortical connectivity. A subgroup of MDD patients completed a six-week antidepressant follow-up with repeat MRI. A significant interaction between depression and CRP was identified in the left rostral middle frontal cortex (LRMF). FiCD in the LRMF was significantly lower in MDD patients than controls and negatively correlated with CRP in patients but not controls. Following six weeks of antidepressant treatment, FiCD in LRMF increased significantly, and this increase was negatively correlated with baseline. Peripheral inflammation is possibly associated with disrupted cortical connectivity in MDD and disturbs the brain structural recovery process during antidepressant treatment. The left rostral middle frontal cortex possibly serves as an important target.

item.title: Altered language network microstructure links with impaired language function and development in very preterm/very low birth weight born adults.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Premature birth is associated with impaired language function. In premature-born children, language function has been linked with microstructural alterations of the language network.Whether these brain-language associations persist into adulthood remains unclear. We investigated the microstructural properties of major dorsal and ventral language pathways in very preterm/very low birth weight (VPT/VLBW) adults and their associations with language performance in adulthood and childhood. Sixty-three VPT/VLBW and eighty full-term-born adults (mean age 26.8 years) underwent diffusion-weighted imaging and language assessment. The arcuate fasciculus, superior longitudinal fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus were reconstructed using probabilistic tractography from which fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) measures were extracted. Adult language function was assessed via the Regensburg word fluency test, rapid automatized naming and verbal IQ; childhood language was assessed at the mean age of 8 using the Kaufman Assessment Battery for children. We observed altered language network microstructure in VPT/VLBW participants, illustrated by lower FA and higher MD in the SLF and UF. These microstructural alterations were associated with language function in adulthood, but also with language development in childhood. We found that the association between tract microstructure and language abilities differed between groups. Our results demonstrate altered language network microstructure in premature born adults, which links with impaired language function and development. These findings extend previous work by comprehensively characterizing the adult dorsal and ventral language network and relating its microstructural properties to language function across development. The selective follow-up sample may limit generalizability to the broader VPT/VLBW population.

item.title: Treatment-associated structural connectome reorganization following high-frequency rTMS in major depressive disorder: A low- and high-order connectivity study.
item.description:
Journal of psychiatric research
Background High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is an established treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), but associated changes in structural-connectome topology remains unclear. Specifically, higher-order structural connectivity (HOSC), defined by similarities between regional structural connectivity profiles, may provide information beyond direct low-order structural connectivity (LOSC). Methods Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data were acquired from 23 patients with MDD before and after 10-Hz rTMS and from 30 matched healthy controls (HCs). LOSC networks were constructed based on deterministic tractography, whereas HOSC networks were derived from similarities between regional LOSC profiles. Graph-theoretical analysis and network-based statistics were employed to characterize topological and subnetwork differences. Results Depressive symptoms decreased significantly after treatment. Global LOSC topology remained stable, whereas HOSC showed case-control differences in network segregation and post-treatment differences in small-world organization relative to HCs. Network-based analysis revealed focal strengthening of a left insula-hippocampal-inferior temporal component in LOSC and distributed HOSC variation involving cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuitry, particularly the thalamus and caudate. Nodal analyses further identified treatment-associated centrality changes involving the thalamus and hippocampus. Conclusion High-frequency rTMS treatment was associated with coordinated structural-connectome variation across low- and high-order network organization in MDD. These findings should be interpreted as treatment-associated changes rather than effects attributable specifically to rTMS and suggest that HOSC may provide a complementary representation of network variation accompanying clinical improvement.

item.title: Right putaminal gray matter change tracks psychomotor recovery after accelerated iTBS in melancholic treatment-resistant depression.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background Psychomotor retardation is a prominent and disabling feature of melancholic depression. Accelerated intermittent theta-burst stimulation (aiTBS) may hasten antidepressant effects, but neural substrates of early symptom improvement remain unclear. Given the central role of frontostriatal circuitry in motivation and behavioral activation, structural alterations in the striatum may represent a possible neural substrate of early therapeutic change. Methods Structural MRI was acquired from 61 patients with melancholic TRD and 77 healthy controls, and voxel-based morphometry was used to assess baseline striatal gray matter volume differences. Patients then underwent a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial of left dorsolateral prefrontal aiTBS, comprising 20 sessions over four days. In 50 patients with complete pre- and post-treatment data, we tested whether GMV change in the baseline-identified striatal region was associated with clinical change in the active and sham groups (n = 25 each). Results Patients showed greater right putamen GMV than controls at baseline. After active aiTBS, greater right putamen GMV increase was associated with greater psychomotor retardation improvement. This association was absent after sham stimulation and was not observed for overall depression severity. Conclusion The right putamen appears structurally altered in melancholic TRD. After active aiTBS, short-term putamen GMV increase was associated with psychomotor rather than broader depressive improvement. This pattern should not be interpreted as structural normalization but may reflect a relationship between putaminal change and early psychomotor recovery.

item.title: Mapping the brain signature of dyslexia risk onto histamine, acetylcholine and glutamate receptor systems
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
The brain differences of dyslexia are well described and its genetic risk is now measurable; the brain systems that connect the two are unknown. That link decides which measures complement one another in early identification and which systems intervention research should examine. Here we compared large-scale polygenic score maps of brain structure in dyslexia with normative maps of brain neurotransmitter systems. The structural signature of genetic liability aligned with the cortical distribution of neurotransmitter systems. The strongest and most consistent alignment appeared for the histamine H3 receptor, the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) and the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor. The alignment was most pronounced in cingulate, medial and superior frontal cortex and the paracentral lobule. The H3 alignment held after adjustment for cortical position and for metabolic and cognitive reference maps. Once the component common to all nineteen maps and position were removed together, no individual system remained significant, while the shared component itself aligned with liability. The signature therefore follows the topography these systems share. In 169 children, per-person alignment with the H3 map related to reading skill with the opposite sign to liability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to relate the structural signature of genetic liability for dyslexia to normative maps of neurotransmitter receptor and transporter density. It places that signature within the shared geography of the systems that set attention, arousal and synaptic plasticity during learning, and gives the genetics of dyslexia a testable biological axis.

item.title: Beyond the Percentile: CDC-referenced BMI-for-Age and Brain Structure Across Childhood and Adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Importance Pediatric obesity affects 1 in 5 US children and has been linked to brain structural differences. Most evidence is cross-sectional and models body mass index (BMI) linearly, with metrics that compress severe obesity. Objective To examine associations between brain structure and BMI-for-age across the weight spectrum and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) weight status categories, distinguishing between- and within-person associations, and their age and sex moderation. Design, Setting, and Participants Longitudinal cohort study of youth aged 8–10 years at baseline in the US community-based Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (4 waves, 2016–2025; ages 8–18 years). Exposures Extended CDC BMI-for-age z-score, grouped by wave-mean z-score: underweight (<5th percentile, n=297), healthy weight (5th–<85th, n=7,452), overweight (85th–<95th, n=1,919), and obesity (≥95th, n=1,842). Main Outcomes and Measures Cortical thickness (12 regions) and subcortical volume (7 regions) from T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), defined a priori. Results Among 11,510 participants contributing 32,212 observations (mean [SD] age, 12.6 [2.5] years; 52.2% male), higher between-person BMI-for-age z was associated with lower frontal and temporal thickness (6 regions) and larger subcortical volume (5 regions; all q < .001), but associations were nonlinear (17 of 19 regions). Youth with obesity had lower thickness than healthy weight youth in 8 frontal and temporal regions (largest, −0.21 SD; q < .001), with dorsal frontal differences decreasing across adolescence; underweight youth had smaller subcortical volumes. Higher BMI-for-age z was associated with larger subcortical volume (all 7 regions) within the healthy weight category and lower cortical thickness (11 of 12 regions; fusiform: β = −0.27; q < .001) within the obesity category, steeper than in healthy weight youth in 10 regions, but not in overweight or underweight youth. Within-person associations did not reproduce the obesity associations, reversed from negative at age 10 to positive at age 16, and were more negative in female than male participants. Conclusions and Relevance Youth with obesity had lower cortical thickness than healthy weight peers, but associations between brain structure and BMI-for-age differed between CDC weight status groups, suggesting a complex relationship between adiposity and brain structure. Key Points Question How is BMI-for-age associated with brain structure across the weight spectrum, within CDC weight status categories, and within individuals over time in youth? Findings In this cohort study of 11,510 youth aged 8–18 years, those with obesity had lower frontal and temporal cortical thickness than healthy weight youth. Within categories, higher BMI-for-age was associated with lower thickness in obesity but larger subcortical volumes in healthy weight youth; within individuals over time, the obesity association was not reproduced. Meaning BMI–brain associations differ between CDC weight status categories and may be obscured by assuming a single linear association.

item.title: Spatial Patterns of White Matter Hyperintensities and Cognitive Function in Older Adults: A Community-Based Study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Objectives White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are associated with cognitive decline in older adults. We examined whether anatomically defined spatial WMH patterns are associated with cognitive performance and subsequent decline in a large community-based cohort with approximately six years of follow-up. Methods We analyzed 1,667 participants (mean age 76 years) from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study. WMH were segmented from FLAIR images and mapped to 112 white matter regions using deep-learning-based parcellation. Principal component analysis identified dominant WMH distribution patterns; candidate components were selected by Horn’s parallel analysis and retained if stable across resampled split samples. Linear mixed-effects models examined associations between WMH patterns and cognitive performance at baseline and follow-up, adjusting for demographic, genomic, and vascular risk factors. Robustness was assessed using analyses accounting for total WMH burden, study center, and selective attrition. Results Of 14 candidate principal components (PCs) identified by parallel analysis, eight met the resampling stability criterion and were retained, together explaining 42% of the variance. Three components were associated with cross-sectional or future cognition. PC3, characterized by deep white matter burden in the corpus callosum and anterior corona radiata with relative preservation of superficial white matter, showed no cross-sectional association at baseline but was associated with accelerated decline across multiple domains. Interpretation A deep spatial pattern of WMH loading on the corpus callosum and anterior corona radiata was associated with subsequent cognitive decline in the absence of a cross-sectional association at baseline, independent of total lesion burden.
